div.p: . . . had they not by their onset set her free; nor would Gaius Duilius, Aulus Atilius, and Lucius Metellus have delivered her from the terror of Carthage; nor would the two Scipios have quenched with their own blood the rising conflagration of the Second Punic War; nor, when it blazed up again with greater forces, would Quintus Maximus have sapped its strength, or Marcus Marcellus crushed it, or Publius Africanus, having torn it from the very gates of this city, driven it back within the enemy's walls. As for Marcus Cato, a man unknown and new—the very pattern by which all of us who pursue these same ends are drawn toward industry and virtue—he assuredly might have enjoyed his leisure at Tusculum, a healthful spot and near at hand. But the man was mad, as those people reckon it: though no necessity compelled him, he chose to be tossed amid these waves and tempests into extreme old age rather than to live most agreeably in that tranquillity and repose. I pass over the countless men who have each been the salvation of this commonwealth; and because they stand not far from the memory of our own age, I forbear to name them, lest anyone complain that he or one of his own has been left out. This one thing I lay down: so great is the necessity of virtue that Nature has set in the race of men, and so great the love of defending the common safety that she has given, that this force has conquered all the enticements of pleasure and ease.
[Pliny, Natural History, preface 7] . . . nor to the most learned. "I do not wish a Manius Persius to read these things; I wish a Junius Congus."

When all were burning with eagerness to hear, Scipio began to speak thus: "This is a saying of old Cato—whom, as you know, I loved beyond all others and most greatly admired, and to whom, by the judgment both of each of my fathers and by my own zeal, I gave myself wholly from my youth; whose discourse could never sate me. So great was the man's experience of public affairs, which he had conducted both at home and on campaign with the greatest skill and likewise for the longest time; and there was measure in his speaking, a charm mingled with weight, and the highest zeal both for learning and for teaching, and a life thoroughly accordant with his words.
[Nonius, 301M] There is, then, something turbulent in single men, which either exults with pleasure or is broken by distress.
[Nonius, 500M] And the mind itself, which sees the things to come, remembers the things past.

[Augustine, City of God, 2.21; Nonius, 417M] "On ancient manners and on men the Roman state stands," says Ennius—a verse which, whether for its brevity or for its truth, seems to me to have been uttered by him as though from some oracle. For neither would the men, had not the state been so charactered, nor the manners, had not these men presided, have been able either to found or so long to maintain a commonwealth so great and ruling so far and wide. And so, before our own memory, both the ancestral custom itself supplied excellent men, and excellent men kept the old custom and the institutions of their forefathers. But our own age, having received the commonwealth like a splendid picture now fading with age, has not only neglected to renew it with the same colours it had, but has not even taken care to preserve at least its outline and, as it were, its last lineaments. For what remains of those ancient manners on which he said the Roman state stood? which we see so worn away by oblivion that they are not only not cultivated, but already unknown. And what shall I say of the men? For the manners themselves have perished through the want of men, of which so great an evil we must not only render account, but in some sort plead our cause as though on a capital charge. For it is by our own vices, not by any chance, that we retain the commonwealth in word, but in fact have long since lost it.
[Nonius, 42M] You look, then, for the whole foresight of this director, which has gained this very name from "providing" beforehand.
[Nonius, 321M] . . . and that nature herself not only would invite, but even compel it.

Nor indeed is it enough to possess virtue, as though it were some art, unless you use it; for an art, even when you do not employ it, can still be retained as knowledge, whereas virtue consists wholly in its use; and its greatest use is the governance of the state and the achievement, in fact and not in talk, of those very things which those people are forever proclaiming in their corners. For nothing is said by the philosophers—nothing, that is, that is rightly and honourably said—which has not been brought forth and confirmed by the men who have established law for their communities. For whence comes piety, or from whom religion? Whence the law of nations, or this thing we call civil law? Whence justice, good faith, fairness? Whence shame, self-restraint, the flight from baseness, the craving for praise and for honour? Whence courage in toils and dangers? Surely from those who have shaped these things by training, confirmed some of them by custom, and sanctioned others by law.
[Nonius, p. 426M] Thus, since our country contains more benefits, and is an elder parent than he who begot us, surely a greater gratitude is owed to her than to a parent.

He was wont to say, for this reason, that the constitution of our state excelled all other states: because in those others there had generally been single men, each of whom had established his own commonwealth by his laws and institutions—as Minos among the Cretans, Lycurgus among the Lacedaemonians, and among the Athenians, whose constitution had very often been changed, now Theseus, now Draco, now Solon, now Cleisthenes, now many others; and at last, when it was now bloodless and prostrate, the learned man Demetrius of Phalerum propped it up—whereas our own commonwealth was framed not by the genius of one man, but of many, nor in the lifetime of a single man, but over several ages and generations. For he used to say that no genius so great had ever existed, that nothing should escape it, nor could all the geniuses brought together into one foresee so much at one time as to embrace all things without the practice and the lapse of time.
[Nonius, 364M] But as they themselves . . . put their spirit to the test, they see what they think they will do.

. . . favour. How fitly the orders are distinguished—the ages, the classes, the cavalry, in which the votes of the senate too are included—now that too many men foolishly desire this advantage to be done away, who seek some new largess by way of returning the horses through a plebiscite.

[Gellius, Attic Nights, 7.16.11; Nonius, 290M] And this was the greater for this reason, that, when the colleagues were in an equal case, they were not only not equal in odium, but even the affection felt for Gracchus turned aside the odium felt against Claudius.
[Diomedes, GL 1.339K] . . . let him strive.

Indeed they relate that Xenocrates, among the most distinguished of philosophers, when asked what his disciples gained, answered that they came of their own accord to do what they would be compelled to do by the laws. That citizen, then, who compels all men by the authority of his command and the penalty of the laws to do what the philosophers can scarcely persuade a few to do by their eloquence, is to be preferred even to the teachers who debate these matters. For what discourse of theirs is so refined that it ought to be set above a well-ordered state with its public law and customs? For my part, just as I judge that "great and imperious cities"—as Ennius calls them—are to be preferred to hamlets and forts, so I hold that those who preside over these cities by their counsel and authority are far to be set above, in point of wisdom itself, those who have no share in any public business. And since we are above all swept toward enlarging the resources of the human race, and strive by our counsels and labours to render the life of men safer and richer, and are spurred to this delight by the very goads of Nature, let us hold to the course that has always been the course of every best man, and let us not heed those signals that sound the retreat, to call back even those who have already gone forward.
[Nonius, p. 526M] Nor would Carthage have held such great resources for some six hundred years without counsel and discipline.

Wherefore, as he was wont, so now shall my discourse trace the origin of our people; for I gladly use even the word of Cato. And I shall more easily attain what is proposed, if I show you our commonwealth being born, and growing, and come to maturity, and now firm and robust, than if I myself, as Socrates does in Plato, should fashion some imaginary state of my own."

. . . and to vehicles against slowness; and the same Reason, when it had received men uttering something inchoate and confused in unshaped voices, broke these up and distinguished them into parts, and, as it were tokens, stamped words upon things, and bound together by the most delightful bond of speech men who before had been disjoined. By a like exercise of mind, the sounds of the voice, which seemed infinite, were all marked and expressed by the finding of a few signs, whereby both conversations with the absent, and the tokens of men's wills, and the records of things past might be kept. To this was added number, a thing both necessary to life and, alone, unchangeable and eternal; which first impelled us also to look up to the sky, and not in vain to gaze upon the motions of the stars, and by the reckonings of nights and of days . . .
[Nonius, 431M] The Carthaginians first, by their trafficking and their wares, imported into Greece avarice and ostentation and the insatiable cravings of all things.
[Servius, on Aeneid 5.546] . . . that guardians were wont to be given to those going out to military service, by whom in the first year they should be governed.

. . . that nothing is so kingly as the unfolding of fairness, in which lay the interpretation of right—the right which private men were wont to seek from kings; and for these causes wide and fertile lands of plough-land and orchard and pasture were marked out, to be the king's and to be cultivated without the king's toil and labour, that no care of private business might draw him away from the affairs of the peoples. Nor indeed was any private man an arbiter or judge of a suit, but all things were settled by the king's judgments. And to me at least our Numa seems most of all to have kept this old custom of the kings of Greece. For the rest, although they too discharged this office, yet for a great part waged wars and tended the rights of war; but that long peace of Numa was the mother of right and of religion to this city—he who was even a writer of laws, which you know are extant, a thing indeed proper to that citizen of whom we are treating . . .

[Eulogius, on the Dream of Scipio, 401Or.] . . . who, having been set upon the pyre, came to life again and told many secrets of the world below . . . that these things which are said about the immortality of the soul and about heaven are not the inventions of dreaming philosophers, nor incredible fables such as the Epicureans deride, but the conjectures of prudent men.
[Diomedes, GL 1.374K] . . . they excel.

Against these reasons, so sure and so plain, are set, by those who argue the contrary side, first the labours that must be sustained in defending the commonwealth—a slight hindrance, surely, to a man vigilant and industrious, and one to be scorned not only in such great matters but even in middling pursuits or duties or indeed in private business. Added to this are the perils of life, and the disgraceful dread of death is held up against brave men—men to whom it generally seems more wretched to be wasted by nature and old age than to be granted the time in which they might render up that life, which must in any case be rendered to Nature, above all for their country. And in this passage they think themselves copious and eloquent, when they gather up the calamities of the most illustrious men and the wrongs heaped upon them by ungrateful fellow citizens.
[Nonius, p. 276M] "I would learn, by Hercules," he said, "that habit and zeal of yours for discourse."

When all had approved this, "What have we," he said, "as the beginning of a constituted commonwealth, so clear and so well known to all, as the founding of this city, set on foot by Romulus? Who, born of his father Mars (for let us grant the report of men—especially one not only of old standing, but also wisely handed down by our ancestors, that men well-deserving of the common good should be thought to be of divine descent, and not only of divine genius)—he, then, as soon as he was born, with his brother Remus, is said to have been ordered by Amulius, king of Alba, through fear of the overthrow of his kingdom, to be exposed by the Tiber; in which place, when he had been suckled at the dugs of a beast of the woods, and shepherds had taken him up and reared him in rustic ways and toil, he is reported, when he had grown up, to have so excelled the rest both in bodily strength and in fierceness of spirit, that all who then dwelt in those fields where this city now stands obeyed him willingly and with a glad heart. When he had offered himself as their leader with their forces—to come now from fables to facts—he is said to have crushed Alba Longa, a city strong and powerful in those times, and to have slain King Amulius.

. . . whose minds raised themselves higher and were able to do or to devise something worthy of the gift, as I said before, of the gods. Wherefore let those men who discourse of the principle of living be for us great men, as they are, let them be learned, let them be masters of truth and virtue—provided only there be this thing, whether discovered by men engaged in the variety of public affairs, or also handled in the leisure and writings of those others, a thing, as it is, by no means to be despised: the civil principle and the discipline of peoples, which, in good natures, accomplishes what it has already very often accomplished, that an incredible and well-nigh divine virtue should arise.
[Scholiast on Juvenal, Satires 10.362] That Sardanapallus, far more deformed by his vices than by the very name.

. . . a grown youth to be stripped. So deeply have the foundations, as it were, of modesty been laid. But the training of youth—how absurd it is in the gymnasia! how trifling that soldiery of the ephebes! how loose and unrestrained their handlings and loves! I pass over the Eleans and the Thebans, among whom in the love of free-born youths lust has even a licence permitted and unrestrained; the Lacedaemonians themselves, though they concede everything in the love of young men save defilement, fence off by a thin wall indeed that which they except; for they permit embraces and lying together, with cloaks set between. Here Laelius: "I understand clearly, Scipio, that in those Greek disciplines which you blame, you prefer to wrestle with the most noble peoples rather than with your own Plato, whom you do not even touch upon, especially since . . .
[Nonius, 497M] But yet, as a good father of a family must have some practice of cultivating, of building, of reckoning . . .
[Augustine, City of God, 22.28] . . . that he wished rather to be understood as having played than to affirm that this is true.

For from this come those famous examples among the Greeks: that Miltiades, conqueror and subduer of the Persians, when the wounds he had taken full in the breast in that most glorious victory were not yet healed, poured out in the chains of his fellow citizens the life he had saved from the enemy's weapons; and that Themistocles, driven and harried from the very country he had set free, fled not to the ports of Greece which he had himself preserved, but to the bosom of that barbarian land which he had crushed. Nor indeed are there lacking examples of the fickleness and cruelty of the Athenians toward their greatest citizens; and these, born and grown common among them, are said to have overflowed even into our own most august state.

[Lactantius, Divine Institutes, 3.16.5] Surely all the disputation of those men, though it contains the most plentiful springs of virtue and knowledge, yet, set beside their deeds and accomplishments, makes me fear it may seem to have brought men not so much business as delight.

Having won this glory, he is said first to have thought of founding the city under the auspices and of establishing a commonwealth. As for the site of the city, which must be most diligently provided for by him who tries to plant a lasting commonwealth, he chose it with incredible advantage. For he did not bring it down to the sea—which, with that band and those forces, was most easy for him—so as to advance into the territory of the Rutuli and the Aborigines, or himself to found a city at the mouth of the Tiber, in which place King Ancus many years later led out a colony; but this man, with surpassing foresight, perceived and saw that maritime sites are not the most advantageous for cities founded in the hope of lasting long and of empire; first, because maritime cities are exposed not only to many dangers, but also to hidden ones.

But if anyone has thought that to those instruments of the mind which he held both by nature and by civil institutions, there should be joined for himself also learning and a fuller knowledge of things—as do those very men who are engaged in the discussion of these books—there is no one but ought to set them before all others. For what can be more splendid than when the handling and the practice of great affairs is joined with the studies and knowledge of those arts? Or what more perfect can be conceived than Publius Scipio, than Gaius Laelius, than Lucius Philus? who, that they might leave out nothing which pertains to the highest praise of illustrious men, joined to the manner of their home and their ancestors this learning too, brought in from Socrates.
[Priscian, GL 2.255K] . . . unless someone wishes to fashion Athos from the foundations into a monument. For what Athos or Olympus is so great?
[Nonius, 362M] And our Plato even more than Lycurgus, who bids absolutely all things to be common, lest any citizen be able to call any thing his own or proper to himself.

. . . to come to know roots and seeds—will that offend you?" Manilius: "Not at all, if only there be need of it." Scipio: "Do you think this is the bailiff's business?" Manilius: "By no means; since the tilling of the field very often lacks labour." Scipio: "Then, as the bailiff knows the nature of the field, the steward knows letters, but each turns himself from the delight of knowledge to the usefulness of accomplishing—so let this our director have studied, by all means, the knowledge of right and of the laws, and have at least looked through into their springs, but let him not hinder himself by answering questions and reading and writing, that he may be able, as it were, to manage the commonwealth and in it to act as a kind of bailiff—a man most skilled in the highest law, without which no one can be just, not unacquainted with the civil law, but only so far as the steersman is acquainted with the stars, the physician with natural things; for each uses those to his own art, yet does not hinder himself from his own office. But this man will see . . .
[Servius, on Aeneid 6.877] Fannius, it is a hard cause to praise a boy; for it is not the achievement that is to be praised, but the promise.

For one recalls the exile of Camillus, or the affront to Ahala, or the odium against Nasica, or the expulsion of Laenas, or the condemnation of Opimius, or the flight of Metellus, or the most bitter ruin of Gaius Marius and the slaughter of leading men, or the destruction of those many that followed soon after. Nor indeed do they now spare my own name; and, I suppose because they think themselves preserved in that life of ease by our counsel and our peril, they complain of us all the more grievously, and the more lovingly. But I could not easily say why, when they themselves cross the seas for the sake of learning or sightseeing . . .
[Arusianus Messius, GL 7.457K] From which those men were drawing them away.

For the mainland gives warning beforehand, by many signs and by a kind of crash and the very sound, of the approach of enemies, whether expected or even sudden; nor indeed can any enemy come flying by land, but that we may know not only that he is, but also who he is and whence. But that maritime and naval enemy can be present before anyone can suspect he is coming; nor indeed, when he has come, does he show beforehand who he is, or whence he comes, or even what he wants; in short, not even any mark can be discerned or judged, whether he be at peace or an enemy.

Wherefore he who both wished and was able to do both—that is, to furnish himself both with the institutions of his ancestors and with learning—him I reckon to have attained everything that belongs to praise. But if one or the other of two ways of prudence must be chosen, yet, even though that quiet manner of life amid the best studies and arts will seem to some the happier, this civil life is assuredly the more praiseworthy and the more illustrious, by which life the highest men are so adorned, as either Manius Curius, 'Whom no one could surpass by steel or gold,' or . . .

[Nonius, 24M] The judgment of the censor brings to the condemned man scarcely anything but a blush. And so, since all that adjudication turns only upon his name, that animadversion has been called ignominy.

. . . in those states in which the best men seek praise and honour and flee disgrace and dishonour. Nor indeed are they so much terrified by fear and the penalty which is appointed by the laws, as by that sense of shame which nature has given to man, as it were a kind of dread of a censure not unjust. This the director of commonwealths increased by men's opinions, and perfected by institutions and disciplines, so that shame should keep the citizen from misdeeds no less than fear. And these things indeed pertain to praise, which could have been said more widely and more fully.

[Lactantius, Divine Institutes, 1.18.11] "If it is right for any man to ascend within the regions of the heavenly ones, for me alone the greatest gate of heaven lies open" . . . "It is so indeed, Africanus; for to Hercules too that same gate lay open."

. . . that I had, on laying down the consulship, sworn in the assembly before the Roman people, while they swore the same, that the commonwealth was safe, I should easily set off against it the care and trouble of all my wrongs. And yet my own fortunes brought more honour than toil, and not so much vexation as glory; and I took greater joy from the longing of good men than grief from the gladness of the wicked. But had it fallen out otherwise, as I said, how could I complain? Since nothing had befallen me unforeseen, nor heavier than I had expected, in return for such great deeds of mine. For I was a man who, though it was open to me to reap greater fruits from leisure than others, on account of the varied sweetness of the studies in which I had lived from boyhood, or, should anything more bitter befall the community at large, to undergo no special but only an equal share with others of fortune's lot, did not hesitate to set myself in the way of the most violent tempests and almost of the very thunderbolts, for the saving of my fellow citizens, and by my own private perils to purchase the common ease for the rest.

There is, moreover, in maritime cities a certain corruption and degeneration of manners; for they are mingled with new tongues and ways of life, and there are imported not only foreign wares, but also foreign manners, so that nothing can remain unspoiled in the institutions of the fathers. Now those who inhabit such cities do not cling to their own seats, but are forever snatched far from home by winged hope and imagining; and even when they remain in body, yet in mind they are exiles and wanderers. Nor indeed did any thing more overthrow both Carthage and Corinth at last—long shaken—than this straying and dispersal of the citizens, who, through the desire of trade and seafaring, had forsaken the cultivation of their fields and of arms.

. . . to have been wisdom; yet there was this difference in the principle of each kind, that those nourished the first principles of nature by words and arts, while these did so by institutions and laws. But this one state of ours has produced more such men—if fewer wise men, since they hold that name so strictly, yet surely men worthy of the highest praise, since they cultivated the precepts and discoveries of the wise. And further, of how many states are there that are to be praised, and that have been—since this is in the nature of things by far the greatest task of counsel, to establish a commonwealth that may be lasting—if we count single men into single states, what a multitude of excellent men is even now found! And if we should wish to survey in mind either the Latium of Italy, or its Sabine or Volscian people, if Samnium, if Etruria, if that great Greece, if then the Assyrians, if the Persians, if the Carthaginians, if these . . .

[Nonius, 24M] For I do not wish the same people to be the ruler and the toll-gatherer of the world. And the best revenue, both in private households and in the commonwealth, I reckon to be thrift. For good faith—fides—seems to me to have its very name from the fact that what is said is done—fit.

But for the life and the conduct of living, that principle has been ordained in lawful marriages, in legitimate children, in the holy abodes of the household gods and of the family Lares, that all might use both the common advantages and their own; nor can one live well without a good commonwealth, nor can anything be happier than a well-constituted state. Wherefore it is wont to seem most strange to me, what is the so great learning . . .

[Seneca, Letters, 108.32sq.] "in very deed" . . . "of his own self" . . . Since we have been called back from the very goal by his interruption . . . "for whom no citizen nor enemy was able to render a fit recompense for his deeds."

For our country did not bring us into being or rear us under any such law that she should look for no nourishment, as it were, from us, and, serving only our conveniences, supply a safe refuge for our ease and a quiet resting place for our repose; but rather that she might pledge to herself, for her own use, the most numerous and the greatest portions of our mind, our talent, and our judgment, and leave to us for our own private use only so much as might be left over for herself.

Many incitements too to luxury, ruinous to states, are furnished by the sea, things either taken or imported; and the very pleasantness of the place has many enticements of the passions, either costly or slothful. And what I said of Corinth, I know not but that one might most truly say of all Greece; for the Peloponnese itself is almost wholly in the sea, nor, save the Phliuntians, are there any whose fields do not touch the sea; and outside the Peloponnese, only the Aenianes and the Dorians and the Dolopians are away from the sea. What shall I say of the islands of Greece? which, girt by the waves, almost float themselves together with the institutions and manners of their states.

. . . And Philus: "A splendid cause indeed you bring to me, when you wish me to undertake the advocacy of wickedness." "And yet you must beware," said Laelius, "that, if you say those things which are wont to be said against justice, you may seem even to think so—you who are yourself, as it were, the one example of ancient probity and good faith, and whose habit of arguing on the contrary sides is not unknown, since you think the truth is thus most easily found." And Philus: "Well then," he said, "I will humour you, and bedaub myself knowingly; since those who seek gold do not think this should be refused them, surely we, when we seek justice, a thing far dearer than all gold, ought to flee no trouble. And would that, as I am about to use another's speech, so it were permitted me to use another's mouth! Now those things must be said by Lucius Furius Philus which Carneades, a Greek and accustomed to whatever was convenient, used to argue in words . . .

[Nonius, 430Msq.] I admire the elegance not only of the matter, but also of the words. "If they wrangle," he says. The contention of well-wishers, not the strife of enemies, is called wrangling . . . The law, then, holds that neighbours wrangle with one another, not litigate.

[Cicero, Letters to Atticus, 8.11.1] For as to the steersman a prosperous voyage, to the physician health, to the commander victory, so to this guide of the commonwealth the happy life of the citizens is set as his goal—that it be firm in resources, rich in means, ample in glory, honourable in virtue; for of this work, the greatest and best among men, I wish him to be the accomplisher.

[Macrobius, Saturnalia, 1.4.2sq.] But although to the wise the very consciousness of noble deeds is the amplest reward of virtue, yet that divine virtue desires no statues fixed in lead, no triumphs with withering laurels, but certain more lasting and greener kinds of rewards. "What, pray, are these?" said Laelius. Then Scipio: "Suffer me, since we have now kept holiday for the third day . . .

[Anonymous, Paradoxa, Koronne, Bielowski] Whosoever win for themselves the esteem of men by feasts and banquets and lavish spending, plainly show that they lack that true honour which is born of virtue and worth.

As for those refuges that they seize for their own excuse, the more freely to enjoy their ease, these surely are by no means to be listened to: when they say that for the most part men come into public life who are worthy of no good thing, that to be compared with them is sordid, and to contend with them—especially when the multitude is roused—is wretched and dangerous; and therefore that it is not the part of the wise man to take the reins, since he cannot curb the mad and ungoverned impulses of the crowd; nor the part of a free man, struggling with foul and monstrous adversaries, to submit to the lash of insults or to await wrongs not to be borne by a wise man—as though there were any juster cause for good and brave men of lofty spirit to approach the commonwealth than this: not to be subject to the wicked, nor to suffer the commonwealth to be torn apart by them, while they themselves, even should they wish, were unable to bring aid.

And these things indeed, as I said above, belong to old Greece. But of the colonies led out by the Greeks into Asia, Thrace, Italy, Sicily, Africa, which is there—save the one Magnesia—that the wave does not wash? Thus a kind of shore of Greece seems woven, as it were, upon the fields of the barbarians; for of the barbarians themselves none were formerly maritime, save the Etruscans and the Carthaginians—the one for the sake of trade, the other of piracy. The cause of the evils and the changes of Greece is plain, namely those faults of maritime cities which I touched on briefly a little before. Yet in these faults there is that great convenience: that whatever is produced anywhere may come by sea to the city you inhabit, and that what its own fields bring forth they can carry and send to whatever lands they will.
[Nonius, 263M] . . . that you may answer Carneades, who is wont often to make sport of the best causes by the trickery of his wit.

[Augustine, City of God, 2.14] To these, when there is added the shout and approval of the people, as of some great and wise master, what darkness do they spread, what fears do they bring in, what cravings do they inflame!
[Augustine, City of God, 5.13] . . . that he must be nourished by glory . . . that their ancestors did many wondrous and splendid things through the desire of glory.

When I had come into Africa, as you know, a tribune of the soldiers to the consul Manius Manilius, attached to the fourth legion, nothing was more to my mind than that I should meet King Masinissa, for just causes most friendly to our family. When I came to him, the old man embraced me and wept, and a little after looked up to heaven and said: "I give thanks to thee, most high Sun, and to you, the rest of the Heavenly Ones, that before I depart from this life I behold, in my kingdom and beneath these roofs, Publius Cornelius Scipio, by whose very name I am revived; so never does the memory of that best and most unconquered man depart from my mind." Then I asked him about his kingdom, and he me about our commonwealth, and with many words bandied back and forth on either side that day was spent for us.
[Codex ms., note 458, p. 82, Ossolineum Library] . . . that good faith must be shaken gently and calmly, not by force and onset . . .

[Lactantius, Divine Institutes, 6.8.6] There is indeed a true law, right reason, agreeing with nature, diffused among all, constant, everlasting, which calls to duty by commanding, and deters from fraud by forbidding; which yet neither commands nor forbids the good in vain, nor moves the wicked by commanding or forbidding. Here Scipio: "I will do what you wish, as I can, and will enter upon the discussion by that rule which I believe must be used in discussing all things, if you would remove error: that, of the matter about which the inquiry is to be made, if it is agreed what its name is, it should be explained what is meant by that name; and if this be agreed, then at last it will be fitting to enter upon the discourse. When Laelius had approved, "Yet I shall not so discuss," said Africanus, "a matter so illustrious and so well known, as to go back to those elements which learned men are wont to use in these matters—to begin with the first union of male and female, then with offspring and kinship, and to define more than once what each thing is and in how many ways each is spoken of; for when I speak among prudent men, who have been engaged with the highest glory in war and peace in the greatest commonwealth, I will not bring it about that the very matter about which I discourse should be less illustrious than my speech. Then Laelius: "For my part, I look forward to that very kind of speech which you promise."

"The commonwealth, then," said Africanus, "is the affair of a people; but a people is not every gathering of men assembled in any way whatsoever, but a gathering of a multitude joined together by an agreement upon law and by a sharing of advantage. And the first cause of their coming together is not so much weakness as a certain natural, as it were, herding instinct in men; for this race is not solitary nor given to wandering alone, but so begotten that, even amid an abundance of all things . . .

. . . eighteen with the highest census-rating. This arrangement, were it unknown to you, I should unfold; but as it is, you see that the principle is such that the centuries of the knights, with their six votes, and the first class, with a century added which was given to the carpenters for the highest service of the city, hold eighty-nine centuries; to which, if out of the hundred and four centuries (for so many remain) only eight be added, the whole force of the people is completed; and the much greater remaining multitude of ninety-six centuries was neither shut out from the votes, lest it be arrogant, nor too powerful, lest it be dangerous.

Moreover, by the accensi velati, the trumpeters, the horn-blowers, the proletarii . . .

[Lactantius, Divine Institutes, 5.18.4] Virtue plainly wills honour, nor is there any other reward of virtue . . . Which, however, she receives readily, and exacts not bitterly . . . . . . certain seeds, as it were; nor is there found any institution either of the other virtues or of the commonwealth itself. These gatherings, then, established for the cause I have set forth, first fixed their seat in a certain place for the sake of dwellings; and when they had fenced it with natural defences and by their own labour, they called such a joining of dwellings a town or a city, marked out with shrines and with common spaces. Every people, therefore, which is such a gathering of a multitude as I have described, every state, which is the constitution of a people, every commonwealth, which, as I said, is the affair of a people, must be governed by some counsel, that it may be lasting. And this counsel must always be referred, first of all, to that cause which begot the state.

[Nonius, p. 342M] . . . that a commonwealth is established in the best condition which, blended in due measure of those three kinds—the royal, the aristocratic, and the popular—does not provoke by punishment the savage and fierce spirit.

. . . in Asia Tiberius Gracchus persevered toward the citizens, but neglected the rights and treaties of the allies and of the Latin name. And if this habit and licence shall begin to flow more widely, and shall lead over our empire from right to force, so that those who hitherto obey us of their own will are held by terror—even though for us, who are of that age, the watch is nearly over, yet I am anxious concerning our posterity and concerning that immortality of the commonwealth, which could be perpetual, if it were lived by the institutions and manners of the fathers.

Then it must be entrusted either to one man, or to certain chosen men, or undertaken by the multitude and by all. When, therefore, the supreme control of all things lies in the hands of one man, we call that one a king, and the condition of that commonwealth a kingdom. When it lies with the chosen, then that state is said to be ruled by the will of the best men. And that is a popular state (for so they call it) in which all things are in the people's hands. And any one of these three kinds, if it holds fast that bond which first bound men together in the fellowship of a commonwealth, is not indeed perfect, nor in my judgment the best, but tolerable nonetheless—so that one may be more excellent than another. For either a just and wise king, or chosen and leading citizens, or even the people itself—though this is least to be approved—can yet seem, if no inequities or cupidities come between, to stand in a condition that is not unstable.

. . . sixty-five years older, in that it was founded thirty-nine years before the first Olympiad. And that most ancient Lycurgus saw nearly the same things. And so that equability, and this threefold kind of commonwealth, seems to me to have been common to us with those peoples. But what is proper to our commonwealth—than which nothing can be more splendid—that I will pursue, if I can, more closely; and it will be of such a sort that nothing like it is to be found in any commonwealth. But in kingdoms the rest have too small a share in the common law and counsel, and under the rule of the best men the multitude can scarcely have any part in liberty, since it lacks all share in common counsel and power; and when all things are done through the people, however just and moderate it be, yet that very equality is itself unjust, since it admits no degrees of rank. And so, though Cyrus that Persian was a most just and most wise king, yet the affair of the people—for that, as I said before, is the commonwealth—does not seem to me to have been most desirable, when it was ruled by the nod and at the will of one man; and though the Massiliots, our clients, are ruled with the utmost justice by chosen and leading citizens, yet there is in that condition a certain likeness of servitude in the people; and though the Athenians, at certain times, when the Areopagus had been done away with, did nothing save by the votes and decrees of the people, yet, since they had no distinct degrees of rank, their state did not keep its proper ornament.

For in a commonwealth in which there is one man of perpetual power, especially royal, although there be in it also a senate—as there was at Rome when there were kings, as at Sparta under the laws of Lycurgus—and although there be some right of the people too, as there was under our kings, yet that royal name stands out, nor can a commonwealth of this kind not both be and be called a kingdom. And that form of state is most changeable for this cause: that, hurled headlong by the fault of one man, it most easily falls into the most ruinous part. For the royal kind of state in itself is not only not to be blamed, but I am inclined to think it far to be preferred to the other simple kinds, if I should approve any simple kind of commonwealth at all—but only so long as it keeps its own condition. And that condition is, that the safety and the equability and the ease of the citizens be ruled by the perpetual power and justice and all the wisdom of one man. Much, in general, is lacking to that people which is under a king, and chiefly liberty—which lies not in having a just master, but in having none . . .

. . . to bring back. Therefore who would call that the affair of a people—that is, the commonwealth—when all were oppressed by the cruelty of one man, and there was no single bond of right, nor agreement nor fellowship of the gathering, which is a people? And the same thing at Syracuse. That splendid city, which Timaeus calls the greatest of Greek cities and the fairest of all—its citadel worth seeing, its harbours flowing in even to the bosom of the town and to the foundations of the city, broad streets, porticoes, temples, walls—all these availed nothing the more, while Dionysius held it, to make it a commonwealth; for nothing belonged to the people, and the people itself belonged to one man. Therefore where there is a tyrant, there one must say there is, not a faulty commonwealth, as I said yesterday, but, as reason now compels, plainly no commonwealth at all.

And I speak of these three kinds of commonwealth as not disturbed and mingled, but as keeping their own form. These kinds first have, each one, the faults I named before; then they have other ruinous faults; for there is no kind of those commonwealths which has not a sheer and slippery path to a certain neighbouring evil. For under that king, to name him above all—tolerable, or, if you will, even lovable, Cyrus—there lies, ready for the licence of a mind once changed, that most cruel Phalaris, into whose likeness the rule of one man slips by an easy and downhill course. And to that administration of the state by the few and the leading men of the Massiliots, there is a neighbour in that conspiracy and faction of the Thirty which once existed among the Athenians. And the power of the Athenian people itself over all things—not to seek others—turned to the frenzy and licence of the multitude, a plague . . .

. . . they bore. For indeed that unjust and bitter master was for some while attended by prosperous fortune in his doings. "Splendidly indeed you speak," said Laelius; "for I now see whither your discourse tends." Scipio: "And most rightly indeed you judge; for what was then the affair of the Athenians, when, after that great Peloponnesian War, those thirty men presided most unjustly over the city? . . . the worst; and from this either the rule of the best men or that factious tyranny, or kingly or even very often popular rule, and likewise from that one of those kinds I named before is wont to flower forth; and wondrous are the cycles and as it were the revolutions in commonwealths of changes and alternations. To recognize these is the part of a wise man; but to foresee them when they impend, guiding the course in the steering of the commonwealth and keeping it in his own power, is the part of some great and almost divine citizen. And so I judge that there is a certain fourth kind of commonwealth most to be approved, which is moderated and blended from those three I first named.

Here now will be turned that cycle, whose natural motion and revolution learn to recognize from the beginning. For this is the chief thing in civil prudence—in which all this our discourse is engaged—to see the paths and turnings of commonwealths, that, when you know whither each thing inclines, you may be able either to hold it back or to meet it beforehand. For that king of whom I speak, first, stained with the murder of an excellent king, had not a sound mind; and since he himself feared the utmost punishment for his crime, he wished himself to be feared; then, propped by victories and riches, he exulted in insolence, and could govern neither his own manners nor the lusts of his household.

Scipio: "I come now to that third kind, in which perhaps there will seem to be difficulties. And so, when his elder son had offered violence to Lucretia, daughter of Tricipitinus, wife of Collatinus, and the modest and noble woman had, for that wrong, punished herself with death, then a man pre-eminent in genius and virtue, Lucius Brutus, threw off from his fellow citizens that unjust yoke of harsh servitude. Do you see, then, how from a king there arose a master, and how, by the fault of one man, the kind of commonwealth was turned from good into worst? For this is that master of the people whom the Greeks call a tyrant; for they will have him to be a king who takes thought, as a parent, for his people, and preserves those over whom he is set in the best possible condition of living—a truly good kind of commonwealth, as I said, but yet inclined and as it were prone to the most ruinous condition.

Here Scipio: "I recognize," he said, "that habit of yours, Spurius, averse from the cause of the people; and although it can be borne more mildly than you are wont to bear it, yet I assent that of these three kinds none is less to be approved. But this I do not assent to you, that the best men are to be preferred to a king; for if it is wisdom that governs the commonwealth, what, pray, does it matter whether this be in one man or in several? But we are deceived by a certain error in arguing thus; for when the term 'best men' is used, nothing can seem more excellent—for what better can be conceived than the best?—but when mention is made of a king, there occurs to the mind even an unjust king. But we say nothing now of an unjust king, since we inquire about the royal commonwealth itself. Wherefore think of Romulus, or Pompilius, or Tullius as king; perhaps you will not so much repent of that commonwealth."

. . . when in the people some one or several had become richer and more opulent, then, from their disdain and pride, they relate that it arose—the cowardly and weak giving way, and yielding to the arrogance of the rich. But if the people hold fast their own right, they deny that anything is more excellent, freer, happier; since they are masters of the laws, the courts, war, peace, treaties, and the life and money of each man. This alone, they think, can rightly be called a commonwealth, that is, the affair of a people. And so it is the custom for the affair of a people to be claimed into liberty both from the domination of kings and from that of the fathers, while kings are not sought from free peoples, nor the power and resources of the best men.

For as soon as this king bends himself into a more unjust domination, he becomes straightway a tyrant, than whom no living thing more foul, more hideous, more hateful to gods and men can be conceived; who, though he is in shape a man, yet by the monstrousness of his manners surpasses the most savage beasts. For who would rightly call that man a man, who wishes for himself no fellowship of law with his fellow citizens, no, no fellowship of humanity with the whole race of men? But there will be for us another fitter place of speaking on this kind, when the matter itself shall have admonished us, to speak against those who, even when the state was already freed, sought after dominations.
