And indeed they deny that this whole kind of free people ought to be rejected on account of the fault of an ungoverned people; that, when the people is of one mind and refers all things to its own safety and liberty, nothing is more unchangeable, nothing more firm; and that concord is easiest in that commonwealth in which the same thing is profitable to all; that from the varieties of advantage, when one thing benefits some and another others, discords arise; and so, when the fathers held control, the state's condition was never settled; and far less so in kingdoms, of which, as Ennius says, 'there is no sacred fellowship nor good faith in kingship.' Wherefore, since law is the bond of civil fellowship, and the right of the law is equal, by what right can a fellowship of citizens be held together when the condition of the citizens is not equal? For if it is not pleasing that monies be equalized, if the talents of all cannot be equal, the rights at least of those who are citizens in the same commonwealth ought to be equal among themselves. For what is a state but a fellowship in law? . . .

You have, then, the first origin of a tyrant; for this name the Greeks willed to be that of an unjust king; but our people called all those kings who held sole and perpetual power over peoples. And so both Spurius Cassius and Marcus Manlius and Spurius Maelius are said to have wished to seize the kingship, and lately Tiberius Gracchus . . .

. . . As for the other commonwealths, they think they ought not even to be called by those names by which they would wish themselves to be called. For why should I call by the name of Jupiter Most High a man greedy of domination or of sole command, lording it over an oppressed people—why not rather a tyrant? For a tyrant can be as merciful as a king can be harsh; so that this is the only difference to peoples, whether they serve a courteous master or a harsh one; but that they serve at all cannot be otherwise. And by what means could that famous Lacedaemon attain, in the time when the discipline of its commonwealth was thought to excel, to having good and just kings, when whoever was born of royal stock had to be held king? As for the best men, who could endure those who have arrogated this name to themselves, not by the people's grant, but by their own assemblies? For how is that man judged 'best'? By learning, by accomplishments, by pursuits . . .

. . . Lycurgus called the elders gerontes at Lacedaemon—too few of them, indeed, twenty-eight, in whose hands he wished the chief counsel to be, while the king held the chief command; whence our people, following and interpreting that same thing, named those whom he had called old men the senate, as we have said Romulus did when the fathers had been chosen; yet there stands out and is pre-eminent the force, the power, and the name of the king. Impart even to the people some share of power, as did both Lycurgus and Romulus; you will not sate it with liberty, but you will kindle in it the desire of liberty, when you have given it but a taste of power; yet always will that fear impend, lest the king, as for the most part happens, prove unjust. Fragile, then, is that fortune of a people which is set in the will or the manners, as I said before, of one man.

. . . if it does this by chance, it will be overturned as quickly as a ship, if one drawn by lot from among the passengers takes hold of the helm. But if a free people chooses those to whom it commits itself—and it will choose, if only it wishes to be safe, all the best men—then surely the safety of states is set in the counsels of the best, especially since nature has so ordained it, not only that the highest in virtue and in spirit should preside over the weaker, but that these also should be willing to obey the highest. But they say that this best condition has been overthrown by the perverse opinions of men, who, through ignorance of virtue—which, being in few, is judged and discerned by few—think that wealthy and well-supplied men, or men born of noble family, are the best. And when, through this error of the crowd, the resources of a few, and not their virtues, have begun to hold the commonwealth, those leaders cling tooth and nail to the name of the best men, but in fact are without the name. For riches, name, resources, empty of counsel and of any measure of living and of commanding others, are full of disgrace and of insolent pride; and there is no uglier form of a state than that in which the most opulent are thought the best.

Wherefore let this be the first form and aspect and origin of a tyrant, found by us in that commonwealth which Romulus founded under the auspices—not in that which, as Plato wrote, Socrates himself depicted for himself in that threefold discourse; so that, as Tarquinius, having gained no new power, but using unjustly that which he had, overthrew this whole kind of royal state, let there be set against him another, good and wise and skilled in the advantage and dignity of the citizens, as it were the guardian and steward of the commonwealth; for so let him be called, whoever shall be the director and helmsman of the state. See that you recognize this man; for he it is who by counsel and effort can protect the state. And since this name is as yet less worn in our discourse, and the kind of this man must be handled more often in the rest of our speech . . .

But when virtue governs the commonwealth, what can be more splendid? When he who commands others is himself slave to no cupidity; when he has himself grasped all those things to which he trains and summons the citizens, and lays no laws upon the people which he does not himself obey, but sets his own life before his fellow citizens as a law. If such a one could by himself attain all things sufficiently, there would be no need of more; if all together could see the best and agree upon it, no one would seek chosen leaders. The difficulty of taking counsel transferred the affair from a king to several; the error and rashness of peoples transferred it from the multitude to a few. So, between the weakness of one and the rashness of the many, the best men have held the middle place, than which nothing can be more moderate; and while these protect the commonwealth, peoples must needs be most happy, freed from all care and reflection, their ease left to others whose duty it is to guard it and not to suffer it to come about that the people should think its own advantages neglected by its leaders.

. . . he sought out, and he wrought a state to be wished for rather than to be hoped for—the smallest he could make it, not such as could exist, but one in which the principle of civil things might be discerned. But I, if in any way I can attain it, will strive, by the same principles which he saw, not in the shadow and image of a state, but in the greatest commonwealth, so to touch the cause of each public good and ill as with a wand. For when those royal forty years and a little more than two hundred had passed, with the interregna, and Tarquinius had been expelled, so great a hatred of the royal name held the Roman people as the longing for Romulus had held them after his death, or rather his departure. And so, as then they could not bear to be without a king, so, Tarquinius being driven out, they could not bear to hear the name of king. Here, when the opportunity . . .
53fr. [Nonius, 526M] . . . And so that splendid constitution of Romulus, when it had stood firm for about two hundred and twenty years . . .

For as to that equality of right which free peoples embrace, it can neither be preserved (for the peoples themselves, however loosed and unbridled, yet grant much to many, and there is among them a great choosing of men and of dignities), and that which is called equality is most unjust. For when equal honour is held by the highest and the lowest—who must needs exist in every people—that very fairness is most unfair; which cannot happen in those states which are ruled by the best men. These things, in general, Laelius, and certain others of the same kind, are wont to be argued by those who most praise this form of commonwealth."

. . . that whole law was abolished. With this mind our ancestors then both expelled the innocent Collatinus, through the suspicion of kinship, and the rest of the Tarquins, through the offence of the name; and with the same mind Publius Valerius both first ordered the rods to be lowered, when he had begun to speak in the assembly, and brought his own house down beneath the Velia, after he perceived that, because he had begun to build in a higher place of the Velia, in that very spot where King Tullus had dwelt, the people's suspicion was being stirred; and the same man—in which Publicola was most himself—carried to the people that law which was the first passed in the centuriate assembly, that no magistrate should put to death or scourge a Roman citizen against his appeal.

Then Laelius: "What of you, Scipio?" he said; "of those three, which do you most approve?" Scipio: "You ask rightly, which of the three I most approve, since I approve none of them by itself, taken separately, and I set before any single one of them that which has been blended together from all. But if some single and simple form must be approved, I should approve the kingly. . . first . . . in . . . is called in this place, there occurs the name, as it were paternal, of a king, as of one taking thought for his fellow citizens, as for those born of himself, and preserving them more zealously than . . . to be sustained by the diligence of one best and highest man.

That appeal lay even from the kings the pontifical books declare, our augural ones too signify, and likewise that it is permitted to appeal from every judgment and penalty the Twelve Tables indicate in several laws; and the fact that it is handed down to memory that the decemvirs, who wrote the laws, were created without right of appeal, shows clearly enough that the other magistrates were not without appeal. And the consular law of Lucius Valerius Potitus and Marcus Horatius Barbatus, men wisely popular for the sake of concord, sanctioned that no magistrate be created without right of appeal; nor indeed did the Porcian laws, which are three, of the three Porcii, as you know, bring anything new save the sanction.

There are present the best men, who profess that they do this same thing better, and say there will be more counsel in several than in one, and yet the same fairness and good faith. But behold, with mightiest voice the people cries out that it will obey neither one nor a few; that nothing, even to wild beasts, is sweeter than liberty; that all are without it, whether they serve a king or the best men. Thus kings capture us by affection, the best men by counsel, peoples by liberty, so that in the comparison it is hard to choose what one would most wish." Laelius: "I believe it," he said; "but what remains can scarcely be unfolded, if you leave this begun and unfinished."

And so Publicola, that law concerning appeal having been carried, at once ordered the axes to be taken from the rods, and the next day chose Spurius Lucretius as his colleague in his stead, and, because he was older, bade his own lictors pass over to him, and was the first to establish that the lictors should walk before the single consuls in alternate months, lest there should be more insignia of command in a free people than there had been under a kingdom. No mean man was this, as at least I understand it, who, by granting the people moderate liberty, the more easily held fast the authority of the leading men. Nor do I now without cause chant to you these things so old and so obsolete, but in illustrious persons and times I define examples of men and of affairs, toward which the rest of my discourse may be directed.

Scipio: "Let us imitate, then, Aratus, who, setting out to speak of great matters, thinks one must begin from Jove." Laelius: "What Jove? Or what has this discourse like to that poem?" Scipio: "Only this," he said, "that we may rightly take from him the beginnings of our speaking, whom all, learned and unlearned, agree to be the one king of all gods and men." "What?" said Laelius. And he: "What do you think, save what is before our eyes? Whether these things were established by the leaders of commonwealths for the use of life—that a single king should be thought to be in heaven, who by his nod, as Homer says, would turn all Olympus, and be held both king and father of all—great is the authority and many are the witnesses, if indeed it is granted that all are to be called many, that the nations have so agreed, plainly by the decrees of their leaders, that nothing is better than a king, since they judge that all the gods are ruled by the will of one; or whether we have learned that these things rest on the error of the unlearned and are like fables, let us hear, as it were, the common teachers of learned men, who have seen as with their eyes those things which we scarcely come to know by hearing." "Who, pray," said Laelius, "are these?" And he: "Those who, by investigating the nature of all things, perceived that this whole universe is by mind . . .

The senate, then, held the commonwealth in this condition in those times, so that in a free people few things were done through the people, most by the authority and institution and custom of the senate; and the consuls held a power annual only in point of time, but in its very kind and right royal. And that which was, for keeping the power of the nobles, the very greatest, was vehemently retained: that the assemblies of the people should not be ratified, unless the authority of the fathers had approved them. And in these very times a dictator too was instituted, about ten years after the first consuls, Titus Larcius; and this new kind of command seemed nearest to the likeness of a king. But yet all the highest matters were held by the leading men with the greatest authority, the people yielding; and great things in those times were waged in war by the bravest men endowed with the highest command, dictators and consuls.

But that which the very nature of things compelled to come about—that the people, freed from kings, should claim a little more right to itself—came to pass after no long interval, in about the sixteenth year, in the consulship of Postumus Cominius and Spurius Cassius; in which there was perhaps a want of reason, but yet the very nature of commonwealths often overcomes reason. For hold fast this, which I said at the outset: that unless there be in a state this balanced compensation of right and of duty and of office—so that there be enough of power in the magistrates, of authority in the council of the leading men, and of liberty in the people—this unchangeable condition of the commonwealth cannot be preserved.

. . . But, if you will, Laelius, I will give you witnesses neither too ancient nor in any way barbarous." Laelius: "Those," he said, "I want." Scipio: "Do you see, then, that this city is less than four hundred years old, in being without kings?" Laelius: "Indeed less." Scipio: "What then? Is this age of four hundred years, for a city and a state, very long?" Laelius: "That is scarcely grown to maturity," he said. Scipio: "Then in these four hundred years there was a king at Rome?" Laelius: "And a proud one, too." Scipio: "What before?" Laelius: "A most just one, and so on backward all the way to Romulus, who was king six hundred years before this time." Scipio: "Then not even he is very ancient?" Laelius: "By no means, and with Greece already almost growing old." Scipio: "Tell me, was Romulus a king of barbarians?" Laelius: "If, as the Greeks say, all men are either Greeks or barbarians, I fear he may have been a king of barbarians; but if that name is to be given by character, not by language, I think the Greeks no less barbarians than the Romans." And Scipio: "And yet, for the matter in hand, we do not inquire about race; we inquire about characters. For if prudent men, and not ancient, wished to have kings, I am using witnesses neither very ancient nor inhuman and savage."

For when the state had been shaken by debt, the plebs first occupied the Sacred Mount, then the Aventine. Nor indeed did the discipline of Lycurgus hold even those Greek men in those reins; for at Sparta too, in the reign of Theopompus, there are likewise five whom they call ephors, and in Crete ten who are called cosmoi, set up against the kingly power, as the tribunes of the plebs against the consular command.

Then Laelius: "I see you, Scipio, well furnished with testimonies; but with me, as with a good judge, arguments avail more than witnesses." Then Scipio: "Use then an argument, Laelius, your own very feeling." "What feeling?" said he. Scipio: "If ever, if by chance, you have seemed to yourself to be angry with someone." Laelius: "Indeed more often than I should wish." Scipio: "What then—when you are angry, do you permit that anger the mastery of your mind?" Laelius: "By Hercules, no," he said; "but I imitate that famous Archytas of Tarentum, who, when he had come to his country house and found everything done otherwise than he had ordered, said to his bailiff, 'Ah, you wretch, I would have flogged you to death by now, were I not angry.'" "Excellently," said Scipio.

There had perhaps been some reason for our ancestors of remedying that debt—a reason which neither had escaped Solon the Athenian not long before, nor, somewhat later, our senate, when, on account of the lust of one man, all the bonds of the citizens were freed and the binding of debtors thereafter ceased; and always for this class, when the plebs, weakened by expenses through a public calamity, was failing, some relief and medicine has been sought for the safety of all. That counsel being then passed over, a cause arose for the people, two tribunes of the plebs being created through sedition, that the power and authority of the senate might be lessened; which yet remained weighty and great, with the wisest and bravest men guarding the state both by arms and by counsel, whose authority most flourished, because, though they far surpassed the rest in honour, they were inferior in pleasures and scarcely superior in wealth; and each man's virtue was the more welcome in the commonwealth, because in private matters they most diligently protected the single citizens by their service, their counsel, their substance.

"So Archytas plainly reckoned anger, dissenting from reason, to be a kind of sedition of the mind, and wished it to be quieted by counsel; add avarice, add the lust for command, add the lust for glory, add the passions; and you see this: that if there be in men's minds a kingly command, it will be the mastery of one—of counsel, namely (for that is the best part of the mind)—and that, with counsel ruling, there is no place for the passions, none for anger, none for rashness." Laelius: "So it is," he said. Scipio: "Do you then approve a mind so disposed?" Laelius: "Nothing more," he said. Scipio: "Then you would not approve, if, counsel being driven out, the passions, which are numberless, or the angers held all things?" Laelius: "Indeed I should reckon nothing more wretched than such a mind, than a man so minded." Scipio: "It pleases you, then, that all the parts of the mind should be under a kingship, and that they should be ruled by counsel?" Laelius: "It pleases me so." Scipio: "Why then do you hesitate what to think about the commonwealth? In which, if the affair be transferred to several, it may now be understood that there will be no command to preside; which, indeed, unless it be one, can be none at all."

In which condition of the commonwealth, Spurius Cassius, who was contriving to seize the kingship—flourishing in the highest favour with the people—a quaestor accused; and him, as you have heard, when his father had said that he had found him guilty in that fault, the people yielding, he put to death. And welcome too was that law, about the fifty-fourth year after the first consuls, concerning fine and pledge, which Spurius Tarpeius and Aulus Aternius, consuls, carried in the centuriate assembly. Twenty years after, because Lucius Papirius and Publius Pinarius, censors, in exacting fines, had diverted from private men into the public store a great quantity of cattle, a light valuation of beasts in the matter of fines was established by the law of the consuls Gaius Julius and Publius Papirius.

Then Laelius: "What, pray, is the difference between one and several, if justice is in the several?" And Scipio: "Since I have perceived, Laelius, that you are not greatly moved by my witnesses, I will not cease to use you as a witness, to prove this which I say." "Me?" said he; "in what way?" Scipio: "Because I noticed lately, when we were at the Formian villa, that you strictly enjoined your household to be obedient to the word of one man." Laelius: "The bailiff, of course." Scipio: "What? At home, do several preside over your affairs?" Laelius: "Nay, but one," he said. Scipio: "What? Does anyone else besides you rule the whole house?" Laelius: "By no means." Scipio: "Why then do you not grant the same in the commonwealth—that the rule of single men, if only they be just, is best?" Laelius: "I am brought," he said, "almost to assent."

But some years before, when the highest authority was in the senate, the people suffering it and obedient, a plan was entered upon, that both the consuls and the tribunes of the plebs should abdicate their magistracy, and that decemvirs of the greatest power, without appeal, should be created, who should both have the highest command and write the laws. And when they had written ten tables with the highest equity and prudence of the laws, they substituted for the following year other decemvirs, whose good faith and justice were not praised in like manner. Yet out of that college there is that signal praise of Gaius Julius, who, when a noble man, Lucius Sestius, in whose chamber he said a dead man had been dug up in his presence, though he himself had the highest power, because being a decemvir he was without appeal, nevertheless demanded sureties, because he said he would not neglect that splendid law which forbade the life of a Roman citizen to be decided save in the centuriate assembly.

And Scipio: "You would assent the more, Laelius, if—to pass over comparisons—I should arrive at greater matters: that it is more right to commit a ship to one helmsman, a sick man to one physician, if only they be worthy of those arts, than to many." Laelius: "And what are these?" Scipio: "What? Do you not see that, through the want of measure and the pride of one man, Tarquinius, the name of king came into hatred with this people?" Laelius: "I see it indeed," he said. Scipio: "Then you see also this—of which, as my discourse goes on, I think I shall say more—that, Tarquinius expelled, the people exulted with a certain wondrous arrogance of liberty; then innocent men were driven into exile, then the goods of many were plundered, then there came annual consuls, then the rods were lowered before the people, then appeals in all matters, then secessions of the plebs, then in short most things were so done that all power was in the people." Laelius: "It is as you say," he said.

A third decemviral year followed, when the same men were in office and had not wished to substitute others. In this condition of the commonwealth—which I have already often said cannot be lasting, because it was not balanced toward all the orders of the state—the whole commonwealth was in the hands of the leading men, the most noble decemvirs being set over it, no tribunes of the plebs set against them, no other magistrates joined, no appeal to the people left against death and scourging.

"It is indeed," said Scipio, "in peace and ease; for one may sport, while one fears nothing, as on a ship, and often even in a light illness. But as that man who sails, when the sea suddenly begins to grow rough, and that sick man, when his disease grows heavy, implore the help of one—so our people in peace and at home commands and threatens its very magistrates, refuses, appeals, calls them to account; but in war obeys as a king; for safety avails more than caprice. And in graver wars our ancestors willed that all command, even without a colleague, should rest in single men, whose very name indicates the force of their power. For a dictator indeed is so called because he is named; but in our books you see him, Laelius, called the master of the people." Laelius: "I see it," he said. And Scipio: "Wisely, then, those men of old . . .

Therefore, from the injustice of these men, there suddenly arose the greatest disturbance and the change of the whole commonwealth; who, two tables of unfair laws being added, by which—the very intermarriages which are wont to be granted even to peoples severed from one another—these men sanctioned by a most inhuman law that the plebs should not have them with the fathers (which afterward was abrogated by the Canuleian plebiscite), presided over the people in every command lustfully and bitterly and greedily. Well known, of course, is that affair, and celebrated in very many monuments of letters: when a certain Decimus Verginius, on account of the intemperance of one of those decemvirs, slew with his own hand his maiden daughter in the forum, and, mourning, fled to the army which was then at Algidus; and the soldiers forsook that war which was on their hands, and first occupied in arms the Sacred Mount, as had been done before in a like cause, then the Aventine . . .
63fr. [Philargyrius, Servius, on Georgics 3.125] . . . Lucius Quinctius having been named dictator.

. . . when the people has been bereft of a just king, 'a longing holds their hearts for long,' as Ennius says, 'after the death of the best of kings'; and at once among themselves they speak thus: 'O Romulus, godlike Romulus, what a guardian of your country the gods begot in you! O father, O begetter, O blood sprung from the gods!' They did not call those whom they justly obeyed masters or lords, nor indeed even kings, but guardians of their country, but fathers, but gods; and not without cause; for what do they add? 'You led us forth to the shores of light.' They reckoned that life, honour, and dignity had been given them by the king's justice. The same will would have remained in their posterity, had the likeness of the kings remained; but you see that, through the injustice of one man, that whole kind of commonwealth fell." Laelius: "I see it indeed," he said, "and I am eager to learn those courses of changes, not more in our commonwealth than in every commonwealth."

When Scipio had said these things, and, all being silent, the rest of his discourse was awaited, then Tubero: "Since these our elders ask nothing of you, Africanus, you shall hear from me what I find wanting in your discourse." "By all means," said Scipio, "and gladly indeed." Then he: "You seem to me to have praised our own commonwealth, when Laelius had asked of you not about our own, but about every commonwealth. Nor yet have I learned from your discourse by what discipline, by what manners or laws we may establish or preserve that very commonwealth which you praise."

And Scipio: "When I have said what I think about that kind of commonwealth which I most approve, I must speak more carefully about the changes of commonwealths, although I think they will least easily come about in that commonwealth. But of this kingly form the first and most certain change is this: when a king has begun to be unjust, that kind perishes on the spot, and that same man is a tyrant, the worst kind, and neighbour to the best; whom if the best men overthrow, as commonly happens, the commonwealth has the second of the three conditions; for it is, as it were, kingly—that is, the paternal counsel of leading men taking good thought for the people. But if the people of itself slay or cast out a tyrant, it is more moderate, so long as it has sense and wisdom, and rejoices in its deed and wishes to guard the commonwealth it has of itself established. But if at any time the people either offered violence to a just king or stripped him of his kingdom, or even—which happens more often—tasted the blood of the best men and laid the whole commonwealth under its own caprice (and do not think that there is any sea or any flame so great that it is not easier to quell than a multitude unbridled by insolence), then comes about that which is splendidly said in Plato, if only I can express it in Latin; it is hard to do, but I will try nonetheless.

Here Africanus: "I think there will soon be for us, Tubero, a fitter place of discoursing about establishing and preserving states; but concerning the best condition I judged that I had sufficiently answered what Laelius had asked. For first I had defined by number three approvable kinds of states, and three ruinous ones, as many, contrary to those three; and that no one of them was the best in itself, but that there excelled the single kinds that which had been moderately tempered out of the three first.

'When,' he says, 'the insatiable throat of the people has grown parched with the thirst of liberty, and, using ill ministers, has drunk in its thirst a liberty not moderately tempered but too unmixed, then it pursues the magistrates and leaders, unless they be very mild and lax and supply liberty to it abundantly; it accuses them, arraigns them, calls them overbearing, kings, tyrants.' For I think these things are known to you." Laelius: "Indeed," said he, "most known to me."

And as for my having used the example of our own state, that availed not for defining the best condition (for that could be done without an example), but that in the greatest state it might be discerned in fact what that was which reason and discourse described. But if you seek the very kind of the best condition without the example of any people, we must use the image of nature, since this image of a city and a people . . .

Scipio: "Then these things follow: 'that those who obey their leaders are harried by that people and called willing slaves; but those who, in magistracy, would be like private men, and those private men who bring it about that there be no difference between private man and magistrate, they extol with praises and load with honours; so that needs must in such a commonwealth all things be full of liberty—that every private house too is empty of any mastery, and this evil reaches even to the beasts; in short, that the father fears the son, the son neglects the father, all shame is gone, so that they may be plainly free; that it makes no difference whether one be citizen or stranger; that the master fears his pupils and fawns upon them, and the pupils despise their masters; that the young take to themselves the gravity of the old, while the old descend to the play of the young, lest they be hateful and burdensome to them; whence it comes that even slaves bear themselves more freely, and wives have the same right as husbands, and in such great liberty even the dogs and horses, the very asses at last, run free in such a way that one must give them the road. So from this boundless licence,' he says, 'this sum is gathered—that the minds of the citizens become so squeamish and soft that, if the least force of authority be applied, they grow angry and cannot endure it; whence they begin to neglect the laws too, that they may be plainly without any master at all.'"

. . . whom I have long sought and to whom I desire to come." Laelius: "A prudent man, perhaps, you seek?" Then he: "That very man." Laelius: "You have, from these very men who are present, a fair store—or, indeed, to begin with yourself." Then Scipio: "And would that there were such, in proportion, out of the whole senate! But yet that man is prudent who, as we have often seen in Africa, sitting upon a huge and vast beast, coerces and rules the beast whithersoever he will, and by a light admonition, not by force, bends that wild creature." Laelius: "I know it, and, when I was your legate, I often saw it." Scipio: "Therefore that Indian or Carthaginian coerces a single beast, and that one tame and accustomed to human ways; but in truth that which lies hidden in the minds of men, and that part of the mind which is called reason, frenzies and tames not one beast nor an easy one to subdue—if ever it accomplishes that, which it very rarely can. For both that fierce thing must be held in check . . .

Then Laelius: "Quite exactly," he said, "you have rendered what was said by that man." Scipio: "And—to return now to the author of my discourse—from this excessive licence, which they alone think liberty, he says that a tyrant springs up, as it were, from a certain stock and is, as it were, born. For as from the excessive power of leaders arises the ruin of leaders, so this too-free people is by liberty itself afflicted with servitude. Thus all excessive things—when, whether in weather, or in the fields, or in bodies, they have been too luxuriant—are generally turned into their contraries; and most of all does this happen in commonwealths, and that excessive liberty falls, both for peoples and for private men, into excessive servitude. And so from this greatest liberty a tyrant is begotten, and that most unjust and harshest servitude. For from this untamed, or rather monstrous, people some leader is generally chosen against those leaders now afflicted and driven from their place—a man bold, foul, recklessly persecuting men often well-deserving of the commonwealth, gratifying the people with what is another's and his own; to whom, because as a private man fears are set against him, commands are given and continued, and he is fenced about even with bodyguards, as Pisistratus at Athens; at last, from those by whom they were brought forward, arise the tyrants of those very men; whom if the good overthrow, as often happens, the state is renewed; but if the bold, then comes that faction, another kind of tyrants, and the same arises also often from that splendid condition of the best men, when some perversity has bent the leaders themselves from the way. So, as it were a ball, the tyrants snatch among themselves the condition of the commonwealth from kings, and from these the leaders or the peoples, and from these the factions or the tyrants; nor is the same form of the commonwealth ever held longer."
[Nonius, 300M] . . . which is fed with blood, which so exults in all cruelty that it is scarcely sated with the bitter deaths of men.

"Since this is so, of the three first kinds the kingly by far excels, in my judgment; but to the kingly itself will be preferred that which shall be made equal and tempered out of the three best modes of commonwealth. For it pleases me that there be in the commonwealth something pre-eminent and kingly, something else imparted and assigned to the authority of the leaders, and certain matters reserved to the judgment and will of the multitude. This constitution first has a certain great equability, which free men can scarcely long do without; then firmness, because those first forms are easily turned into their contrary faults, so that from a king there arises a master, from the best men a faction, from the people a mob and confusion; and because those very kinds are often changed into new kinds—whereas in this joined and moderately blended formation of the commonwealth this does not commonly happen without great faults in the leaders. For there is no cause of change, where each man is firmly placed in his own degree, and there lies nothing beneath into which he may rush headlong and fall.

[Augustine, City of God, 2.21] . . . of things most unlike sounds in concert; and what harmony is called by musicians in song, that in a state is concord, the tightest and best bond of safety in every commonwealth; and this without justice can in no way exist.

But I fear, Laelius and you most friendly and most prudent men, that, if I dwell longer on this kind of thing, my speech may seem to be that of one laying down precepts and teaching, and not of one considering the matter together with you. Wherefore I will enter upon those things which are known to all, but have long been inquired into by us. For thus I decide, thus I think, thus I affirm: that none of all commonwealths is to be compared, whether in constitution or in arrangement or in discipline, with that which our fathers handed down to us, received by them in turn from their ancestors. And this, if it please you—since you wished to hear from me even those things which you yourselves already held—I shall both show of what sort it is, and that it is the best; and, setting forth our own commonwealth as a model, I shall fit to it, if I can, all that discourse which I must deliver concerning the best condition of a state. And if I can hold to this and accomplish it, I shall, in my opinion, have abundantly fulfilled this charge which Laelius has laid upon me."

. . . to be full of justice. Then Scipio: "I assent indeed, and I declare to you that there is nothing we should think yet said about the commonwealth, nor whereby we may advance further, unless it be confirmed not only that that is false, that without injustice it cannot be carried on, but that this is most true, that without the highest justice a commonwealth can in no way be governed. But, if it please you, thus far for this day; let us put off the rest (for enough remains) until tomorrow." And when this had so pleased them, an end of discussing was made for that day.

Then Laelius: "It is your task indeed, Scipio," he said, "and yours alone. For who could better than you speak either of the institutions of our ancestors, since you are yourself of most illustrious ancestors; or of the best condition of a state—which, if we have it, even if not now, then who could be more flourishing than you?—or of taking thought for the future, since you, having driven off the two terrors of this city, have made provision for all time?"
